newsitem.title: CHINA: China urges peace in troubled Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: China urges peace in troubled Cambodia.

text.p: China on Thursday urged Cambodia to find a peaceful solution to the country's warring factions and to prevent a deterioration in the crisis over leadership of the Southeast Asian nation.
But Beijing, treading cautiously among old allies and former foes in the divided nation, said it would not become involved in Cambodia's internal affairs.

"All parties in Cambodia should cherish the current peaceful situation and resolve current problems to prevent a deterioration of the situation," Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang told a regular news briefing.
"China will never become involved in Cambodia's affairs," he said. "This is an internal matter."
He refused to comment further on the crisis sparked when Second Prime Minister Hun Sen deposed First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh on July 6 after two days of fighting.

Cambodia's King Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father, was holding meetings at his Beijing residence on Thursday with three foreign ministers of the Association of South East Asian Nations to discuss the crisis.
The talks were held under a veil of secrecy, requested by the Cambodian king, who reigns but does not rule in Cambodia. He has been in Beijing receiving medical treatment.
China has been closely linked to Cambodian politics for more than a decade.
Beijing was the main military backer of the tripartite guerrilla movement spearheaded by the Maoist Khmer Rouge against Hun Sen's Vietnam-backed government in the 1980s.

China ended support to the resistance alliance on the signing of the 1991 Cambodian peace pact, which it had helped broker as a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council. Chinese soldiers later served in the U.N. peacekeeping force in Cambodia.
Beijing's ties with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) have improved since the CPP joined a coalition government with two non-communist factions after the U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
Analysts said China has been cautious to avoid antagonising either Hun Sen or other factions following the most recent fighting in Cambodia.
China's schism with the Khmer Rouge became permanent when the latter refused to recognise the 1993 elections.
During the 1975-79 rule of the Khmer Rouge, more than one million Cambodians were either murdered as suspected enemies of the new rulers or died from overwork or lack of health care.
